author: Research Agent
text: Offline-first, lightweight mobile apps are the practical norm: Because connectivity and power are intermittent, digital clinical tools succeed when they function fully offline and sync with the cloud when bandwidth is available. Solutions that assume always-on internet face implementation failure in many rural clinics. (confidence: high; source: model knowledge - verify)

author: Research Agent
text: Mixed records environment (paper + EHRs) drives need for flexible ingestion: Many clinics use paper registers and only a subset use electronic medical records (OpenMRS, DHIS2-linked systems); effective tools must accept manual entry, CSV import, simple HTTP APIs and SMS/USSD inputs. (confidence: high; source: model knowledge - verify)

author: Research Agent
text: Task-shifting and CHW integration are central to rural primary care: Triage and first-contact care are often performed by lower-cadre staff (nurses, CHWs); digital assistants that support non-physician decision-makers and provide clear escalation pathways have higher adoption potential. (confidence: high; source: model knowledge - verify)

author: Research Agent

author: Research Agent
text: Demand for explainability and audit trails in clinical AI: Clinicians require transparent reasoning (key features driving triage) and the ability to audit decisions to trust and to support medico-legal defense. (confidence: medium; source: model knowledge - verify)

Eligibility usually requires a clear health impact hypothesis, local partnerships (clinic/district/NGO), and an evaluation plan. author: Funding Advisor
text: Funding narrative: Frame funding asks around measurable clinical impact, risk-reduction steps, and procurement-readiness. For grant and pilot requests: pitch a clear hypothesis (how the AI triage reduces missed urgent cases and reduces unnecessary referrals), an operational pilot plan (2–6 rural clinics or CHW program, offline-first app, integration with referral workflows), and an evaluation plan (pre-specified clinical endpoints, safety monitoring, and ethics approvals). For investors: emphasize de-risking milestones already achieved (working offline prototype, clinician usability testing, MoU with a district/NGO for a pilot), a staged plan to clinical validation and procurement, and an exit path (scale via government procurement or NGO programs). Always highlight explainability, audit logging and data governance built-in to meet growing regulatory scrutiny.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 1 - Cover / Hook: Short description of product and target user: an AI triage assistant for nurse- and CHW-led rural primary-care clinics.; Why now: increasing attention to clinical AI in low-resource settings + need for practical offline tools.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 2 - Problem — What rural clinics face: Triage is commonly done by lower-cadre staff (CHWs, nurses, clinical officers) and must safely escalate urgent cases.; Intermittent power/connectivity, mixed paper + EHR systems, and limited device availability reduce feasibility of conventional clinical AI tools.; Poor data quality from manual entry undermines model performance and clinician trust; regulatory/ethical scrutiny is rising.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 3 - Solution — How the AI triage assistant works (user flow): User flow: CHW/nurse opens offline-first app → collects presenting complaint + vitals on-device (guided forms) → app runs deterministic rules + ML hybrid triage logic → displays recommended urgency level, key rationale, and escalation steps (referral criteria, SMS/phone alert template).; Design choices: hybrid rules + ML for explainability, audit logs for provenance, and simple manual entry / CSV import / minimal API for interoperability.; Decisions supported: urgent vs non-urgent triage, escalation/referral triggers, recommended next action (treat on-site, refer, emergency referral).

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 4 - Typical clinical scenarios (examples): Acute febrile illness: identify red flags for immediate referral vs outpatient management.; Respiratory distress / suspected pneumonia: escalate based on respiratory rate, oxygen saturation (if available), and danger signs.; Maternal triage (antenatal danger signs): prompt timely referral and generate referral slips/SMS alerts to receiving facility.; Each scenario includes: inputs required, logic used, recommended actions, and audit trail of the decision.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 5 - Product architecture & interoperability: Offline-first client (mobile lightweight app) with secure local storage, background sync when bandwidth is available, and a minimal cloud backend for analytics and central updates.; Interoperability: accept manual entry, CSV import and minimal API integrations rather than depending on a single EHR standard to accommodate mixed paper + EHR workflows.; Logging: clinical decision provenance, versioned model/rule IDs and timestamps for auditability.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 6 - Deployment, minimal device/IT requirements & support model: Minimum on-site tech: basic Android devices (phones/tablets) or a shared clinic tablet, intermittent power fallback (battery packs or solar where available) and optional pulse oximeters/thermometers as needed per scenario.; Support model: short on-site training for nurses/CHWs, simple job aids, district-level supervisor onboarding, remote support with periodic on-site refresher visits.; Operations: background sync + lightweight logs to enable supervisor dashboards and district feedback loops.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 7 - Data, privacy, security & offline/low-bandwidth operation: Data sources: on-device collected clinical encounter data, optional CSV imports from registers, limited sync of de-identified data for central analytics.; Consent & governance: built-in informed consent workflow at point of care; audit trails and versioned decision logs for governance and medico-legal traceability.; Security & residency: local encrypted storage while offline, secure sync with transport encryption; design to allow choice of local residency vs central cloud to meet local policy.; Mitigations for poor data quality: structured guided forms, required minimal fields, local validation rules, and supervisor review workflows.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 8 - Map of representative rural clinic workflows & minimum integration touchpoints: Representative flow: patient arrival → triage entry (CHW/nurse) → brief assessment using assistant → on-site management or referral → referral feedback loop to district.; Staffing & touchpoints: single nurse or clinical officer with CHW support; minimum integrations: patient encounter capture (app/manual), referral slip generation (print/SMS), supervisor sync for oversight.; Operational constraints to design for: limited hours, variable staffing ratios, mixed paper registers, intermittent connectivity and device sharing.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 9 - Business model, procurement & go-to-market: Customer segments: small rural primary-care clinics/health posts, district health offices, and district hospital outpatient departments.; Buyer economics & procurement pathways: pilots and procurement often run via foundations, district health bodies, or intermediaries/accelerators; procurement-readiness requires clinical validation and procurement-aligned pilots.; Pricing / reimbursement hypotheses: subscription or per-facility licencing for districts, or grant/contract-funded pilots with transition to procurement; exact pricing and reimbursement model to be validated in pilots.; Pilot-to-scale route: start with 2–6 rural clinics or a CHW program to demonstrate safety, impact and procurement readiness.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 10 - Validation, pilots & regulatory preparedness: Pilot design: measurable hypothesis (e.g., reduce missed urgent cases; reduce unnecessary referrals) and operational pilot in 2–6 rural clinics or CHW program to de-risk clinical AI.; Validation needs: clinical validation, audit trails and consent processes to satisfy ethics committees and procurement bodies.; Funding pathways for pilots: pursue foundation/grant proof-of-concept funds, accelerator support, and early-stage investors for scaling after successful pilots.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 11 - Team, current status & asks (founder to complete): Founders should provide: team bios (clinical lead, product/tech lead, ops/pilot lead), current prototype status, and any existing partnerships with clinics or districts.; Hiring needs and key hires to prepare for pilot (e.g., field ops, clinical validation lead, data security officer).; Risks and mitigation briefly summarized: data quality, clinician trust, regulatory expectations, and connectivity constraints.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 12 - Funding ask, use of funds & next steps: Ask: (founder to specify amount) — proposed use: build pilot-ready product (offline-first app + backend), deploy 2–6 clinic pilot, run clinical validation and procurement-readiness activities, and cover initial ops/support.; Funding route recommendations: apply for foundation/grant pilot funds for the proof-of-concept phase, leverage accelerators for procurement connections, and engage pre-seed angels/impact VCs for follow-on.; Next steps: finalize protocol and budget for pilot, secure pilot partners, and prepare ethics/regulatory materials and consent/audit workflows (verify local requirements).

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 1 - Cover / Hook: Product: offline-first mobile triage assistant (hybrid rules + ML) for nurse- and CHW-led rural primary-care clinics.; Primary value: reduce missed urgent cases, standardise escalation, and produce audit trails for procurement and ethics review.; Why now: increasing attention to clinical AI validation, governance and practical offline tools in low-resource settings.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 2 - Problem — what rural clinics face: Triage is often performed by lower-cadre staff (CHWs, nurses) who must identify and escalate urgent cases safely.; Intermittent power/connectivity and mixed paper + EHR workflows make conventional cloud-first AI impractical.; Poor manual-data quality and rising regulatory/ethics scrutiny undermine clinician trust and procurement decisions.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 3 - Solution — how the assistant works: User flow: CHW/nurse opens offline app → guided form (complaint + vitals) → hybrid rules + on-device model → explainable recommendation (manage, urgent refer, emergency) → printed/SMS referral and audit log.; Design choices: deterministic rules + ML for explainability, versioned decision logs, local encrypted storage, background sync.; Interoperability: manual entry, CSV import, minimal API to fit mixed-paper/EHR environments.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 4 - Clinical scenarios & inputs: Representative scenarios: acute febrile illness (red flags), suspected pneumonia (RR, SpO2, danger signs), maternal triage (antenatal danger signs).; For each scenario the app lists required inputs, decision logic, action and an auditable explanation.; Minimal sensor needs: optional pulse oximeter; core operation requires only basic Android device and manual inputs.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 5 - Product architecture & security: Offline-first mobile client with local encrypted store, background sync and a lightweight cloud backend for aggregate analytics and model updates.; Auditability: versioned rules/models, time-stamped logs and consent capture at point-of-care to satisfy ethics/procurement reviewers.; Security: local encryption, transport encryption on sync, configurable data residency (local-only or centralised) depending on district policy.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 6 - Deployment & operational model (devices, training, support): Minimum on-site tech: basic Android phones/tablet per clinic, battery backup (powerbanks/solar), optional pulse oximeter device per site.; Support model: 1–2 day on-site training for clinicians/CHWs + job aids, district supervisor onboarding, remote support and scheduled on-site refreshers.; Operations: local device management, periodic model/rule updates via background sync, supervisor dashboards for QA and feedback loops.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 7 - Compact pilot protocol summary: Design: 2–6 rural clinics (or one CHW program covering similar catchment) over 6 months to demonstrate safety, feasibility and procurement-readiness.; Primary endpoint: reduction in missed urgent cases (operational definition to be finalised with clinical lead and ethics board). Secondary endpoints: change in referral rate, time-to-referral, data completeness, clinician adherence to recommendations, patient follow-up outcomes.; Data collection: app encounter logs, paper register cross-checks, supervisor audit forms, and post-encounter follow-up phone calls. Field research officers collect and upload de-identified data. Outcomes adjudication: blinded clinical review panel reviewing de-identified encounter records and referral outcomes.

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 8 - 6–12 month timeline with milestones & go/no-go gates: Month 0–1: finalise protocol, secure MOUs/LOIs with pilot sites, submit ethics/regulatory application.; Month 2–3: device procurement & configuration, on-site training, baseline data collection.; Month 4–9: pilot operations and iterative improvements; ongoing M&E and data collection.; Decision gates: after 3 months operational data review — go/no-go if (a) data completeness >= target threshold, (b) no safety signal in blinded review, (c) minimum clinician uptake/adherence met. Final scale decision at pilot end based on pre-specified primary endpoint and procurement-readiness metrics.; Time horizon: pilot 6 months typical; extended 9–12 months if ethics approvals or procurement trials require longer follow-up.

author: Pitch Coach

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 10 - Which funder type for which instrument: Foundation / public-health grant: proof-of-concept grant to cover pilot ops, M&E and ethics (short-term non-dilutive). Target ask: Scenario A or B depending on scope.; Accelerator / implementation partners: non-dilutive support + mentorship and procurement introductions; useful for procurement-readiness and district introductions (Scenario B).; District / Ministry procurement contract or innovation fund: scoped pilot procurement contract to embed the tool in routine workflows (Scenario C; aim to demonstrate procurement-readiness metrics required by buyer).; Seed investors / angels (dilutive): pursue only after pilot demonstrates measurable impact and procurement interest — use for product scaling, commercialisation and hiring (next-stage ask estimated separately).; Founder action: map each funder approach to a concrete ask and required deliverables (e.g., foundation grant to cover pilot ops & M&E for X months; accelerator cohort to cover implementation support & introductions).

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 11 - Procurement-readiness metrics, buyer economics & partner commitments: Procurement-readiness metrics to demonstrate in pilot: per-facility and per-patient cost estimates (model knowledge - verify), clinician time-savings (minutes per encounter saved), escalation/referral accuracy targets, data completeness threshold (e.g., % of required fields captured), and safety (no increase in missed urgent cases).; Buyer economics to articulate: expected per-patient cost vs current pathway, operational savings from faster referral, supervisor time-savings from digital audit trails and reduction in unnecessary referrals.; Partner commitments: plan to secure MOUs/LOIs from pilot clinics and a district health office before applications; show signed LOIs in appendix. (Founder to obtain and insert MOUs/LOIs).

author: Pitch Coach
text: Slide 12 - Team, next-stage funding triggers & verification note: Team asks: clinical lead, product/tech lead, field ops/pilot lead, data security officer — list current bios and key hires required for pilot.; Next-stage funding: after a successful pilot (meeting primary endpoint and procurement interest), consider seed/angel raise to scale product dev, expand to more districts and recruit commercial/business development staff. Estimated next-stage ask and runway should be prepared after pilot; figures here would be model knowledge - verify.; Important: always verify funder eligibility, award sizes and deadlines with funders themselves before applying — funding programs change often.
